issues.item: Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, 'comments on family' is not impossible as a trigger, but paired with the rest of the profile it lacks a clear assault-linked context. The other triggers and memory items point to sensory/intrusive re-experiencing, whereas this item suggests a family-related theme not represented elsewhere in threat, appraisals, or memory.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies a bereavement/loss-focused coping target, but no other selected items indicate death loss or grief as a central aspect of the assault trauma. This maladaptive strategy does not fit the rest of the profile, which centers on assault-related intrusive memory, dissociation, and social avoidance.

vignette: Carl had been a school counselor for over three decades, guiding generations of students through the ups and downs of adolescence. But it was his own life that took a drastic turn five years ago, when he was assaulted by a stranger in a hospital parking garage. The attack left him with physical scars, but it was the memories that lingered, seared into his mind like snapshots. The smell of hospitals still transported Carl back to that moment, the antiseptic scent conjuring up images of bloodied floors and mangled metal. Whenever he caught a whiff of it, the terror would flood back, as if no time had passed at all. Remembering the event brought back the same fear he felt at the time – his heart racing, his breath catching in his throat. He'd recall fragments of the memory suddenly, without warning: the sound of footsteps behind him, the feel of hands grabbing his shoulders. These sudden pieces would appear and disappear just as quickly, leaving Carl disoriented and shaken. As the memories lingered, Carl began to change. He started avoiding people, afraid that getting close to anyone would lead to another assault. Emotional intimacy became a distant memory; he couldn't bear the thought of being vulnerable again. He'd try to deliberately dissociate from his emotions, blanking out whenever someone got too close. His wife, Rachel, noticed the difference first – how Carl would withdraw into himself during conversations, or avoid physical touch altogether. At work, Carl found it increasingly difficult to connect with his students. The smell of alcohol on a student's breath would transport him back to that fateful night, and he'd struggle to focus on the present moment. He began avoiding school events, citing exhaustion or stress as excuses. His colleagues noticed the change too – how Carl seemed distant, preoccupied. As time passed, Carl's avoidance behaviors only intensified the triggers. By shying away from people and intimacy, he was creating a self-reinforcing cycle of fear and isolation. The more he avoided emotional closeness, the more his memories would intrude, unbidden. And with each intrusion, he'd retreat further into himself, convinced that it was the only way to stay safe. It wasn't until Rachel staged an intervention, worried about Carl's increasingly reclusive behavior, that he realized he needed help. As they sat in their living room, surrounded by photos of their life together, Carl finally acknowledged the toll his memories were taking. He feared losing himself completely, becoming a shadow of the man he once was. With a deep breath, he agreed to seek therapy, hoping to break free from the cycle that had consumed him for so long.
